stages.title: 1: Set 1 — Development Environment & Spring Boot Bootstrap
stages.subtitle: Create the first runnable GeoOps slice and carry it from project generation through CI.

steps.title: Choose Maven as the GeoOps build system
steps.why:
• Alright, before we write any GeoOps code, we need to answer a basic question: how is this Java project going to get the extra code it needs and how are we going to build it?
• A real Java application is rarely made only from classes that we write ourselves. For example, later GeoOps needs to receive HTTP requests. We could try to write a web server from scratch, but that would be a huge amount of unnecessary work. Instead, we reuse code that has already been created and packaged for Java applications.
• That reusable external code is called a library. When our project needs one of those libraries in order to work, we call it a dependency.
• Now another problem appears. Who downloads those dependencies? Which versions do we use? How does another developer get the same ones? How does GitHub Actions know what to download later?
• That is why we're choosing Maven.
• Maven is a build and dependency-management tool. It reads a file named pom.xml, downloads the libraries listed there, compiles our Java code, runs tests, and can package the application.
• So the first idea to remember is:
• GeoOps needs reusable code → we declare dependencies in pom.xml → Maven gets them and builds the project.
• That's the reason Maven becomes our build tool before we even create the first Java class.

steps.title: Keep the implementation language on Java
steps.why:
• Now the generator is asking which programming language we want to use.
• A programming language is simply the language we use to write instructions that the computer will eventually execute.
• Spring Boot projects can be written with Java, Kotlin, or Groovy, but this GeoOps project is specifically our Java learning project, so we choose Java here.
• That choice affects the files Spring Initializr creates for us. Our source files will end in .java, and later we'll create classes such as GeoOpsApplication.java, ProjectController.java, and ProjectService.java.
• Those Java files are still human-readable source code. The computer does not execute the text exactly as we type it. Later the Java compiler will convert that source into bytecode that the JVM can run.
• We don't need to learn the whole compiler and JVM story on this screen. For now, the important point is simple:
• we choose Java here because Java is the language we are going to use to build GeoOps.

steps.title: Select Java 17
steps.why:
• Next we have to choose the Java version.
• Why does a version matter?
• Java keeps evolving. New Java releases can add language features, library APIs, and runtime changes. If one machine uses a newer Java version than another machine, code that works on the first machine may fail to compile or run on the second.
• For GeoOps, we're choosing Java 17.
• Later IntelliJ will use a Java 17 JDK, Maven will compile against Java 17, and GitHub Actions will also set up Java 17.
• The JDK is the Java Development Kit. It contains the tools needed to develop Java software, including the Java compiler.
• So this setting is not just a number in a form. We're creating one rule for the whole project:
• developer machine → Java 17
• Maven build → Java 17
• CI build → Java 17.
• Keeping those environments on the same major version prevents version mismatch problems later.

steps.title: Give the application its GeoOps identity
steps.why:
• Now we're giving the project a proper identity.
• Maven projects use values called coordinates so one project or library can be identified clearly.
• The two values to notice here are group and artifact.
• The group is com.atlasgrid. Think of that as the larger namespace or organization name.
• The artifact is geoops. That's the specific project name inside that group.
• Together they identify this Maven artifact as com.atlasgrid:geoops.
• We're also setting the Java package to com.atlasgrid.geoops.
• A package is how Java organizes related classes and avoids name conflicts. Later you'll see lines such as:
• package com.atlasgrid.geoops;
• at the top of our Java files.
• So these fields are not random form values. They decide how Maven identifies the project and how Java organizes the source code we'll create next.

data.name: GeoOps
data.description: Fictional GIS operations platform used for Java/Spring Boot experience learning

steps.title: Add Spring Web
steps.why:
• Now we need GeoOps to talk over the web.
• What does that actually mean?
• Later another program—Postman in our case—will send an HTTP request to GeoOps. HTTP is the standard request-and-response protocol commonly used by web applications and APIs.
• Our plain Java project does not automatically know how to listen on a web port, map URLs to Java methods, or convert Java objects to JSON.
• Instead of building all of that ourselves, we add Spring Web.
• Spring Web is a dependency that gives us the Spring MVC web framework and the pieces Spring Boot needs to run our application as a web service.
• It also works with an embedded Tomcat server. Embedded means the server comes with the application instead of us installing and configuring a separate Tomcat server manually.
• So the reason for this dependency is:
• GeoOps needs HTTP endpoints → Spring Web provides the web framework and server support → later our controller can receive requests such as GET /api/projects.

steps.title: Add Bean Validation
steps.why:
• Our API will eventually accept data from outside the application.
• For example, a client might send a project code, project name, and coordinate reference system.
• But what happens if the client sends an empty project code?
• We need a way to describe basic rules for incoming data.
• That is why we're adding Validation.
• Validation means checking whether input satisfies rules before we continue processing it.
• This dependency gives us annotations such as @NotBlank.
• An annotation is a piece of metadata we place on Java code using the @ symbol. It tells a framework or tool something about that code.
• Later we'll write @NotBlank beside fields in CreateProjectRequest. Spring will then understand that those values must contain text.
• So instead of writing the same manual empty-value checks inside every controller method, we can declare the rule next to the data it belongs to.

steps.title: Add Lombok
steps.why:
• Here we're adding Lombok, so let's first explain why something like Lombok exists.
• Java classes sometimes need repetitive supporting code. A common example is creating a logger field so the application can write useful runtime messages.
• We could write that logger setup manually every time, and there is nothing wrong with doing that.
• Lombok is a library that can generate certain repetitive pieces of Java code for us during compilation.
• In this first GeoOps set, we're going to use @Slf4j.
• @Slf4j is a Lombok annotation that gives the class a logger named log.
• A logger is used to write application messages such as “project created” or error information while the program is running.
• So Lombok is not replacing Java and it is not hiding our business logic. We're using it for one small reason: remove repetitive setup code while keeping the important application behavior visible.

steps.title: Generate the starter project
steps.why:
• Alright, we have now told Spring Initializr what kind of project we want, so we can generate it.
• Spring Initializr is a project generator. It creates the starting folder structure and build file so we don't have to create every directory and configuration file by hand.
• When we press Generate, it prepares a Spring Boot Maven project using the choices we just made.
• There is one historical detail we need to keep honest.
• The simulator currently shows a newer patch release in the Spring Boot 3.3 family, but the original Developer-7 Set 1 project used Spring Boot 3.3.5.
• A patch version is the last number in a version such as 3.3.5. Patch releases usually contain fixes while staying within the same major and minor line.
• Because this course is rebuilding the original Developer-7 project in order, we'll explicitly set 3.3.5 in pom.xml after opening the project in IntelliJ.
• That way we're learning from the actual project history rather than silently changing it.

steps.title: Open GeoOps in IntelliJ
steps.why:
• Now we've moved from the generator into IntelliJ IDEA.
• An IDE—Integrated Development Environment—is an application that puts the common development tools in one place.
• Instead of writing code in one program, compiling it somewhere else, running tests in another window, and browsing files separately, IntelliJ lets us do all of that from one workspace.
• From here we'll create Java files, edit pom.xml, run JUnit tests, use Maven, start Spring Boot, and inspect terminal output.
• Notice that GeoOps is still very small.
• That's intentional.
• We are not opening a finished application and explaining it backwards. We're going to build the same project piece by piece so every new folder and class has a reason to exist.

steps.title: Bind IntelliJ to the Java 17 JDK
steps.why:
• Before writing code, IntelliJ needs to know which Java development kit this project should use.
• That is what the Project SDK setting controls.
• SDK means Software Development Kit. In Java, the JDK is the development kit that contains the Java compiler and the standard Java tools and libraries developers need.
• The compiler is the program that takes our .java source files and turns them into Java bytecode.
• So when we choose Java 17 here, we're telling IntelliJ:
• “Use the Java 17 development tools when working with this project.”
• This matches the Java 17 choice we made in Spring Initializr.
• If IntelliJ used Java 21 while Maven or CI used Java 17, we could accidentally write code that works locally but fails elsewhere. Setting the JDK now keeps our development environment consistent.

steps.title: Create empty pom.xml
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real pom.xml content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates pom.xml as an empty editor tab at pom.xml.
• We deliberately leave pom.xml blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch pom.xml fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Type the canonical GeoOps pom.xml
steps.why:
• Now we're creating the real Maven build file for GeoOps: pom.xml.
• POM stands for Project Object Model.
• You can think of pom.xml as Maven's instruction file for this project.
• It answers questions such as:
• What is this project called?
• Which Java and Spring Boot version are we using?
• Which external libraries does GeoOps need?
• How should Maven package the application?
• At the top, we use the Spring Boot parent version 3.3.5 because that is the original Set 1 baseline.
• Then we declare dependencies for Spring Web, Validation, Actuator, Lombok, and testing.
• Notice that we are not manually writing a version beside every Spring dependency.
• Spring Boot provides dependency management, which means it already knows a compatible group of library versions for that Boot release.
• So instead of guessing which Spring Web, Jackson, Tomcat, and testing versions work together, Maven can use the coordinated versions Spring Boot supplies.

data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>3.3.5</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>
    <groupId>com.atlasgrid</groupId>
    <artifactId>geoops</artifactId>
    <version>0.0.1-SNAPSHOT</version>
    <name>GeoOps</name>
    <description>Fictional GIS operations platform used for Java/Spring Boot experience learning</description>
    <properties>
        <java.version>17</java.version>
    </properties>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-validation</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.projectlombok</groupId>
            <artifactId>lombok</artifactId>
            <optional>true</optional>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

steps.title: Look up Spring Web in Maven Central
steps.why:
• We just wrote dependency names in pom.xml, but the actual library code is not magically inside our repository.
• So where does Maven get it?
• One common place is Maven Central.
• Maven Central is an online repository that stores published Java libraries.
• A repository here does not mean our Git source repository. In Maven terminology, it is a place where packaged Java artifacts can be downloaded.
• When Maven sees a dependency such as Spring Web and that library is not already on the machine, Maven can download the required artifact and its related dependencies.
• Those Java libraries are commonly packaged as JAR files.
• JAR means Java ARchive. It is a packaged file that can contain compiled Java classes and other resources.
• After downloading them, Maven normally stores a local copy under the .m2 repository on the developer machine.
• So the flow is:
• pom.xml names dependency → Maven checks local .m2 → missing artifact is downloaded from a remote repository such as Maven Central → build can use it.
• That's why another developer can clone our project without us committing piles of JAR files into Git.

steps.title: Open the Maven tool window
steps.why:
• Back in IntelliJ, we're opening the Maven tool window.
• Why do we need a Maven window if pom.xml already exists?
• pom.xml is the configuration file. Maven is the build tool. IntelliJ gives us a visual interface for working with that Maven project.
• Here we can see lifecycle phases, dependencies, and Maven goals without typing every command manually.
• But it's important not to confuse IntelliJ with Maven.
• IntelliJ is our IDE.
• Maven is still the tool that understands pom.xml and performs the build.
• That separation matters because GitHub Actions won't be running our local IntelliJ application. It can run Maven directly on another machine.
• So if the Maven build works independently, the project is much easier to reproduce outside our IDE.

steps.title: Walk through the Maven lifecycle
steps.why:
• Now we're looking at the Maven lifecycle, and “lifecycle” simply means the ordered stages Maven can move through while building a project.
• Let's make the reason clear.
• Building a Java application is not one single action.
• First the project needs to be checked, then Java source needs to be compiled, then tests can run, then the compiled application can be packaged.
• Maven gives those stages standard names.
• validate checks the project structure and configuration.
• compile turns main Java source into compiled classes.
• test runs the test code.
• package creates the distributable package, such as a JAR.
• verify performs additional checks after packaging.
• install puts the built artifact into your local Maven repository so other local projects could use it.
• deploy publishes an artifact to a remote Maven repository when a team needs that.
• The useful part is that the phases are ordered. If we ask Maven to run verify, Maven performs the required earlier phases on the way there.
• So later when we run clean verify, we're not invoking a mysterious command—we're asking Maven to rebuild the project and move through the lifecycle up to verification.

steps.title: Create empty GeoOpsApplication.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real GeoOpsApplication.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates GeoOpsApplication.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/GeoOpsApplication.java.
• We deliberately leave GeoOpsApplication.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch GeoOpsApplication.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Type the Spring Boot entry point
steps.why:
• Alright, this is where our GeoOps application actually begins.
• Every running Java application needs some code that starts the program.
• For this application, that starting method is:
• public static void main(String[] args)
• The JVM looks for this standard main method when we launch the class.
• JVM means Java Virtual Machine. It is the runtime that executes Java bytecode.
• Inside main(), we call SpringApplication.run().
• Why do we need that?
• Because we don't want to manually create every Spring object, configure the web server, discover controllers, and wire dependencies ourselves.
• SpringApplication.run() tells Spring Boot to start the application environment for us.
• Now look at @SpringBootApplication.
• This annotation marks this class as the main Spring Boot configuration class. Among other things, it enables automatic configuration and component scanning.
• Component scanning means Spring looks through our package tree for Spring-managed classes such as controllers and services.
• So the startup flow is:
• JVM starts main() → main() calls SpringApplication.run() → Spring creates its application context → embedded Tomcat starts → GeoOps can receive web requests.
• The application can now start, but it still has no GeoOps business data. Next we need an object that represents a project.

steps.title: Create empty GeoProject.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real GeoProject.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates GeoProject.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/project/domain/GeoProject.java.
• We deliberately leave GeoProject.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch GeoProject.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Model one GIS project
steps.why:
• Now we need to answer a basic domain question:
• What information represents one project inside GeoOps?
• A domain object is simply an object that represents something meaningful in the problem our application is solving.
• Here the thing we're modeling is a GIS project.
• For our first version, GeoProject contains an id, project code, project name, coordinate reference system, and creation time.
• The id is a UUID.
• UUID stands for Universally Unique Identifier. It gives each created project its own identifier without us manually choosing numbers such as 1, 2, 3.
• The coordinateReferenceSystem field is important for the GIS domain.
• A coordinate reference system tells us how geographic coordinates should be interpreted. For example, EPSG:4326 is a commonly recognized CRS identifier.
• We're using a Java record because this class mainly carries a fixed group of values.
• And notice what we're deliberately not doing yet: there are no database annotations here.
• Right now the project only needs an in-memory model. We'll introduce persistence only when the learning sequence reaches a real reason for it.

steps.title: Create empty CreateProjectRequest.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real CreateProjectRequest.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates CreateProjectRequest.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/project/api/CreateProjectRequest.java.
• We deliberately leave CreateProjectRequest.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch CreateProjectRequest.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Separate request input from domain state
steps.why:
• Now let's separate the data a client sends from the complete GeoProject object stored by the application.
• Why?
• Imagine a client sends a request to create a project.
• The client should choose the project code, name, and coordinate reference system.
• But should the client also choose the internal UUID and the exact server creation time?
• No. Those values belong to GeoOps itself.
• So we create a separate request object named CreateProjectRequest.
• A request object describes the data expected from the incoming HTTP request.
• Then we place @NotBlank on each required text value.
• Remember the Validation dependency we added earlier? This is where it becomes useful.
• @NotBlank tells the validation system that the value cannot be null, empty, or only whitespace.
• So the responsibility is now clear:
• client supplies projectCode, name, CRS → validation checks them → application creates id and timestamp.
• Keeping those responsibilities separate makes the API easier to control as GeoOps grows.

steps.title: Create empty ProjectService.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real ProjectService.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates ProjectService.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/project/application/ProjectService.java.
• We deliberately leave ProjectService.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch ProjectService.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Add the first GeoOps service
steps.why:
• Now we have data, but we still need somewhere to perform the actual project work.
• We could put everything directly inside ProjectController.
• For a tiny demo, that might seem convenient.
• But think about what would happen as GeoOps grows.
• The controller might start handling HTTP details, project creation rules, duplicate checks, database calls, logging, and other logic all in one class.
• That becomes hard to understand and hard to test.
• So we create ProjectService.
• A service is a class where we place application or business logic that should not live inside the web controller.
• For Set 1, ProjectService has a very simple job: create GeoProject objects and keep them in an ArrayList.
• An ArrayList is a Java collection that stores multiple objects in order.
• We are using it only as temporary in-memory storage because no database exists yet.
• The service also uses @Slf4j. That Lombok annotation gives us a logger, so the earlier Lombok dependency now has a real purpose.
• Our application structure is beginning to separate responsibilities:
• controller will handle HTTP → service will handle project work.

steps.title: Create empty ProjectController.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real ProjectController.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates ProjectController.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/project/api/ProjectController.java.
• We deliberately leave ProjectController.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch ProjectController.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Expose project intake over HTTP
steps.why:
• Now we're giving people or other systems a way to reach GeoOps over HTTP.
• That is the job of ProjectController.
• A controller is a class that receives incoming web requests and decides which application code should handle them.
• @RestController tells Spring:
• “This class contains HTTP endpoints, and the return values should be written into the HTTP response.”
• Then @RequestMapping("/api/projects") gives this controller a base URL.
• Think of it as the common starting address for project-related operations.
• Inside the controller we have two endpoints.
• GET /api/projects asks for the current projects.
• POST /api/projects sends data to create a new project.
• The controller does not contain the project-creation logic itself. It calls ProjectService.
• Why keep that separation?
• Because HTTP handling and business logic change for different reasons.
• The flow is now:
• client request → ProjectController → ProjectService.
• Later, if persistence is introduced, the service can grow without turning the controller into a giant all-purpose class.

steps.title: Create empty application.yml
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real application.yml content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates application.yml as an empty editor tab at src/main/resources/application.yml.
• We deliberately leave application.yml blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch application.yml fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Configure the GeoOps runtime
steps.why:
• Our Java classes describe application behavior, but some values should be easy to change without editing Java source.
• That's why Spring Boot also uses configuration files.
• Here we're creating application.yml.
• YAML is a text format commonly used for configuration. The indentation groups related settings.
• First we set the application name to geoops.
• Then we configure server.port as 8080.
• A port is a numbered communication endpoint on the machine. When our embedded Tomcat server starts on port 8080, a local client can reach it through an address such as http://localhost:8080.
• We're also exposing Actuator health and info endpoints.
• Spring Boot Actuator is a library that provides operational information about a running application.
• The health endpoint gives us a simple question we can ask before testing our own API:
• “Is the GeoOps process up and responding?”
• That will help us separate startup problems from business-API problems in Postman.

data.code:
spring:
  application:
    name: geoops

server:
  port: 8080

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info

info:
  app:
    name: GeoOps
    domain: GIS operations
    company: AtlasGrid Geospatial Systems

steps.title: Create empty GeoOpsApplicationTests.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real GeoOpsApplicationTests.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates GeoOpsApplicationTests.java as an empty editor tab at src/test/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/GeoOpsApplicationTests.java.
• We deliberately leave GeoOpsApplicationTests.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch GeoOpsApplicationTests.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Add a Spring Boot context test
steps.why:
• Before manually clicking through the application, we want at least one automated check that Spring can start with what we've built.
• That is why we're creating GeoOpsApplicationTests.
• A test is code that checks whether some expected behavior is true.
• Here we use @SpringBootTest.
• That annotation tells Spring Boot to create the application context for the test.
• The application context is the container where Spring creates and manages application components such as controllers and services.
• Our contextLoads() method looks almost empty because the test is checking startup itself.
• If Spring cannot build the context because of broken configuration or missing dependencies, the test will fail.
• So this first test answers a very basic but valuable question:
• “Can the current GeoOps application start successfully under test?”
• Later, when we add more business rules, we'll create tests that check those rules directly.

steps.title: Run the JUnit test
steps.why:
• Now let's actually run the test we just wrote.
• JUnit is the testing framework running this Java test.
• A testing framework finds test methods, executes them, and reports whether they passed or failed.
• When contextLoads turns green, it means Spring successfully created the application context during the test.
• That does not prove every future API scenario works.
• It proves the pieces we've built so far are compatible enough for Spring to start.
• This is useful because it gives us a fast checkpoint before we run the whole server and send requests from Postman.
• If this test were red, we would fix the startup problem here instead of debugging several tools at once.

steps.title: Run Maven clean verify
steps.why:
• The test passed inside IntelliJ, but now we want to make sure the project also builds through Maven.
• Why repeat the check?
• Because IntelliJ has its own project environment, while Maven is the build tool our automation will use later.
• We're running:
• mvn clean verify
• clean tells Maven to remove old generated build output from the target directory.
• verify tells Maven to move through the build lifecycle far enough to compile the code, run tests, package the application, and perform verification.
• When we see BUILD SUCCESS, it means the project can be rebuilt using Maven's own process.
• That gives us an important confidence check:
• the code is not only working because of something hidden inside our current IntelliJ session.
• The same Maven command can later run on a clean GitHub Actions machine.

data.console:
[INFO] Compiling GeoOps with Java 17
[INFO] Running GeoOpsApplicationTests
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

steps.title: Start GeoOps from IntelliJ
steps.why:
• Okay, now we're going to run the real GeoOps application.
• Until now we've generated files, compiled code, and executed tests.
• Running the application means starting a live Java process that stays active and waits for requests.
• The JVM starts GeoOpsApplication.main().
• main() calls SpringApplication.run().
• Spring creates the application context and finds classes such as ProjectController and ProjectService.
• Because Spring Web is on the classpath, Spring Boot also configures embedded Tomcat.
• Tomcat starts listening on port 8080.
• So when the console says GeoOps has started, we now have a running server process.
• The important flow is:
• Java process → main() → Spring Boot → Tomcat on port 8080 → HTTP endpoints available.
• Now another program can talk to GeoOps over HTTP, which is why we're moving to Postman next.

data.console: 2026-09-29 INFO Starting GeoOpsApplication using Java 17\n2026-09-29 INFO Tomcat started on port 8080 (http)\n2026-09-29 INFO Started GeoOpsApplication

steps.title: Open the Actuator health request
steps.why:
• Before sending project data, we're going to test the smallest possible thing: whether the application is reachable.
• We're using Postman.
• Postman is an HTTP client, which means it can create HTTP requests and show us the responses a server sends back.
• The request we're opening is:
• GET /actuator/health
• GET is an HTTP method used when a client wants to retrieve information.
• This particular endpoint does not come from our ProjectController.
• Spring Boot Actuator provides it.
• Why start here?
• Because if /actuator/health fails, the problem is probably basic startup, port, or connectivity.
• There would be no reason to debug our project-creation JSON yet.
• So we're checking the foundation first: can Postman reach the running GeoOps server?

steps.title: Confirm GeoOps is healthy
steps.why:
• Now we send the health request and receive:
• 200 OK
• status: UP
• Let's decode that.
• 200 is an HTTP status code. It means the request completed successfully.
• OK is the standard text associated with HTTP 200.
• The JSON response says the application status is UP.
• JSON is a text format commonly used to exchange structured data between systems.
• So this response proves something important:
• Postman was able to send an HTTP request to port 8080, Tomcat received it, Spring Boot handled the Actuator endpoint, and a valid HTTP response came back.
• The path is:
• Postman → HTTP → Tomcat → Spring Boot Actuator → response.
• Now that basic communication works, we can test an endpoint that belongs to our own GeoOps code.

steps.title: Open the Create Project request
steps.why:
• Now we're opening our first real GeoOps business request.
• The HTTP method is POST.
• POST is commonly used when a client wants to send data to create something new.
• The URL is:
• /api/projects
• That matches the base path we placed on ProjectController.
• Look at the JSON body.
• It contains projectCode, name, and coordinateReferenceSystem.
• Those are exactly the fields defined in CreateProjectRequest.
• We're using EPSG:4326 as the CRS value so the example stays connected to GIS work.
• When we send this request, Spring will read the JSON and turn it into a CreateProjectRequest object.
• Then validation can check the @NotBlank rules before ProjectService creates the full GeoProject.
• So this single request is about to connect several pieces we've built separately.

steps.title: Create the first GIS intake record
steps.why:
• Let's send the request and follow what happens instead of just looking at the final response.
• First, Postman sends the JSON over HTTP.
• Tomcat receives the request and Spring routes /api/projects to ProjectController.
• Spring converts the JSON body into CreateProjectRequest.
• Validation checks the required fields.
• The controller then calls ProjectService.
• ProjectService creates a UUID, records the current time, builds the GeoProject, and stores it in the in-memory ArrayList.
• Then the result travels back through the controller and Spring converts the Java object into JSON for the response.
• We receive HTTP 201 Created.
• 201 is the status code normally used when a request successfully creates a new resource.
• So the complete flow is:
• Postman → Controller → validation → Service → GeoProject → in-memory list → JSON response.
• This is the first end-to-end business behavior in GeoOps.

steps.title: Open the project list request
steps.why:
• We just created a project, but we should not assume it was stored correctly.
• So now we're opening:
• GET /api/projects
• This request asks GeoOps to return the projects it currently knows about.
• Because it is a GET request, there is no project JSON body to send.
• Inside the application, Spring routes the request to ProjectController.
• The controller calls ProjectService.findAll().
• The service reads from the same ArrayList where the POST request placed our new GeoProject.
• The method returns a copy of that list rather than handing the original mutable list directly to outside code.
• For the learner, the key idea is simpler:
• POST added one project to memory.
• GET is now going to read that same in-memory state back through the API.

steps.title: Read the project back from GeoOps
steps.why:
• And now we can see the Austin project in the response.
• That proves our first create-and-read round trip works.
• But let's be very clear about what “stored” means in Set 1.
• The project is only stored inside the running Java process, in the ArrayList owned by ProjectService.
• Memory here means the temporary working memory used by the running application.
• If we stop the GeoOps process, that ArrayList disappears.
• When we start the application again, the project list begins empty.
• A database would solve that persistence problem by storing data outside the lifetime of one Java process.
• But we're not adding a database yet because the original learning order has not reached that requirement.
• So the current limitation is intentional:
• running process alive → project exists in memory
• process stops → project is lost.
• That gives us a clean reason for persistence when a later set introduces it.

steps.title: Open the working tree in Git
steps.why:
• Our application works locally, so now we need to record the source-code changes.
• That is where Git comes in.
• Git is a version-control system.
• Version control means keeping a history of how files change over time.
• The working tree you see here is simply the current version of the files on our machine.
• Some files are new because we created them during Set 1.
• Git has noticed those changes, but they are not yet part of a permanent commit.
• Why bother with history?
• Because Set 2, Set 3, and every later set will modify this same project.
• With Git, we can see exactly what changed, return to an earlier state if needed, and share the same history with GitHub.
• So this screen is the bridge between “code currently on my machine” and “code recorded as a project milestone.”

steps.title: Stage the Set 1 files
steps.why:
• Before making a Git commit, we stage the changes we want to include.
• What does staging mean?
• Git separates “files have changed” from “these exact changes should go into the next commit.”
• The staging area is the place where we prepare that next snapshot.
• Think of it like selecting the files you want to put into a package before sealing the package.
• For Set 1, the Java source, pom.xml, configuration, tests, and CI workflow all belong to the same starting milestone.
• So we're staging them together.
• This gives us a chance to review what is about to be recorded before we create the commit.
• The flow is:
• working files → stage selected changes → commit them into Git history.

steps.title: Commit the GeoOps bootstrap
steps.why:
• Now we're creating the Git commit.
• A commit is a saved snapshot in the repository's history.
• We're using the message:
• Complete Set 1 GeoOps bootstrap
• The message explains what this snapshot represents.
• Why is a commit different from simply saving a file in IntelliJ?
• Saving updates the file on your computer.
• Committing records a named point in Git history.
• Later, after Set 2 changes the project, we'll still be able to compare the new code against this Set 1 snapshot.
• That's important for this learning project because we're trying to see how one application evolves, not just collect disconnected final examples.
• So this commit gives us a permanent checkpoint:
• “This is what GeoOps looked like when Set 1 was complete.”

steps.title: Push Set 1 to the remote
steps.why:
• The Set 1 commit currently exists only in our local Git repository.
• If the laptop disappeared, GitHub would not automatically have that new commit.
• So now we push.
• Pushing means sending local Git commits to a remote Git repository.
• Our remote is named origin, and it points to the Developer-7-Intellij repository on GitHub.
• GitHub is a hosted platform that can store Git repositories and add collaboration features around them.
• Once we push main, the remote repository receives our Set 1 history.
• That matters because GitHub Actions can now react to the new commit, and other developers or tools can work from the same repository state.
• So the movement is:
• local files → local Git commit → push → GitHub remote repository.

steps.title: Open Developer-7-Intellij on GitHub
steps.why:
• Now we're looking at the project on GitHub.
• This is the remote repository—the copy of the Git history stored on GitHub rather than only on our machine.
• The repository contains two different kinds of things.
• First, it contains the actual GeoOps project: Java source, Maven configuration, tests, and workflows.
• Second, it contains the curriculum data that tells the learning player which simulator steps to show.
• The reusable simulator software itself is not duplicated here.
• That comes from the separate Experiment-VS-Code repository.
• So the relationship is:
• Experiment-VS-Code → provides the shared simulated software and player.
• Developer-7-Intellij → provides the GeoOps project, learning sequence, and project-specific content.
• Keeping those responsibilities separate means simulator improvements can happen centrally while this repository continues growing the GeoOps project.

steps.title: Open GitHub Actions
steps.why:
• Now we're opening GitHub Actions.
• GitHub Actions is GitHub's automation system.
• An automated workflow is a set of steps GitHub can run when something happens, such as pushing code.
• Why do we need automation if the project already worked on our machine?
• Because “it works on my laptop” is not enough evidence that the repository is healthy.
• A GitHub Actions runner is a fresh machine provided for the workflow.
• Our workflow checks out the code, sets up Java 17, validates the learning curriculum, and runs Maven clean verify.
• CI means Continuous Integration.
• In this project, CI gives us an automatic check every time code is pushed.
• So the important idea is:
• developer pushes code → GitHub starts workflow → clean machine rebuilds and tests project → workflow reports pass or fail.
• That gives us an independent check that the repository can be built from its committed contents.

steps.title: Inspect the successful Set 1 CI run
steps.why:
• This green GitHub Actions run is the final checkpoint for Set 1.
• Let's connect everything we've done instead of treating the green checkmark as magic.
• We used Spring Initializr to create the starting project.
• We opened it in IntelliJ and chose Java 17.
• Maven used pom.xml to manage dependencies and build the code.
• We created the Spring Boot application, domain object, request model, service, controller, configuration, and test.
• JUnit checked that Spring could start.
• We ran the live application and used Postman to call it over HTTP.
• Git recorded the completed source state.
• GitHub received that history.
• GitHub Actions rebuilt and tested the repository on another machine.
• So the full learning path is:
• Spring Initializr → IntelliJ → Java/Spring Boot → JUnit → Maven → Postman → Git → GitHub → GitHub Actions.
• The most important part is continuity.
• Set 2 will modify this exact GeoOps project. We are not going to throw Set 1 away and begin another demo from scratch.

stages.title: 2: Set 2 — System.exit() and Process Boundaries
stages.subtitle: Use a short-lived GIS preflight CLI to learn where process exit belongs and why normal Spring Boot service code must not terminate the JVM.

steps.title: Create empty PreflightResult.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real PreflightResult.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates PreflightResult.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/tools/preflight/PreflightResult.java.
• We deliberately leave PreflightResult.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch PreflightResult.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Model the preflight result before we terminate anything
steps.why:
• Set 2 starts by separating a validation result from the decision to terminate a Java process.
• Our main GeoOps Spring Boot application is a long-running server, but a small dataset preflight check can run as a short command-line program.
• A command-line program is a program launched from a terminal, often with values written after the command as arguments.
• When a command-line process finishes, the operating system needs a simple status value that says whether it succeeded or failed.
• That status value is called a process exit code.
• By convention, exit code 0 means success and a non-zero code represents some kind of failure.
• Later the outer CLI will use System.exit() for failure, but the reusable validation logic should not terminate the JVM by itself.
• System.exit() asks the JVM to stop the entire running Java process, not merely leave one method.
• If validation logic terminated the JVM directly, tests and other callers would lose the chance to inspect the result and choose their own response.
• PreflightResult solves that problem by carrying ordinary data instead of ending the process.
• The valid field tells us whether the dataset passed, exitCode carries the operating-system status we may need later, and message explains the result to a human.
• success() creates a valid result with exit code 0, while failure() stores the specific non-zero failure code.
• The design is now validator → PreflightResult → CLI boundary → process exit only when the outer program decides it is appropriate.

steps.title: Create empty DatasetPreflightValidator.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real DatasetPreflightValidator.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates DatasetPreflightValidator.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/tools/preflight/DatasetPreflightValidator.java.
• We deliberately leave DatasetPreflightValidator.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch DatasetPreflightValidator.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Type the GIS dataset preflight rules
steps.why:
• Now we need the class that actually checks the dataset path supplied to the command-line tool.
• The important design choice is that this validator returns PreflightResult objects and contains no System.exit() call.
• That keeps file-checking logic separate from process-control logic.
• SUPPORTED_EXTENSIONS defines the file types this first preflight version understands: CSV, JSON, and GeoJSON.
• The validate() method receives String[] args, which is the same kind of command-line argument array Java passes into main().
• If there is not exactly one usable argument, we return exit code 2 to mean the command was used incorrectly.
• Path.of() turns the text argument into a Java Path object so the program can work with the filesystem location.
• Files.exists() checks whether something is present at that path; a missing dataset becomes exit code 3.
• Files.isRegularFile() makes sure the path points to a normal file rather than something such as a directory; that failure becomes code 4.
• After that we inspect the filename extension and reject unsupported types with code 5.
• Only after all checks pass do we return PreflightResult.success(), which carries exit code 0.
• Notice the pattern: every branch returns information to its caller instead of deciding to kill the JVM.

steps.title: Create empty GeoOpsPreflightCli.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real GeoOpsPreflightCli.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates GeoOpsPreflightCli.java as an empty editor tab at src/main/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/tools/preflight/GeoOpsPreflightCli.java.
• We deliberately leave GeoOpsPreflightCli.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch GeoOpsPreflightCli.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Put System.exit() at the outer CLI boundary
steps.why:
• This is the class where System.exit() finally belongs.
• GeoOpsPreflightCli is a standalone command-line entry point, so its job includes communicating a final success or failure status back to the operating system.
• main(String[] args) receives the command-line arguments that were typed after the Java command.
• We create DatasetPreflightValidator and ask it to validate those arguments.
• The validator returns a PreflightResult instead of terminating anything.
• If result.valid() is true, we print the success message and simply return from main().
• Returning from main() lets the program end normally, which produces the successful process status without unnecessarily calling System.exit(0).
• If validation failed, we print the error message to System.err.
• System.err is the standard error output stream, normally used for error messages separately from ordinary program output.
• Then System.exit(result.exitCode()) tells the JVM to terminate this short-lived CLI process with the non-zero code selected by the validator.
• This is safe here because the CLI process exists only to perform this one preflight job.
• The same call would be dangerous inside ProjectController or ProjectService because those classes live inside the long-running GeoOps web server JVM.

steps.title: Give Spring Boot time for graceful shutdown
steps.why:
• The web application needs a different shutdown policy from the short-lived CLI.
• A running Spring Boot server can have active HTTP requests and Spring-managed components that should get a chance to finish cleanly.
• A graceful shutdown means the framework stops accepting new work and allows in-progress work a limited amount of time to complete before the process ends.
• Here we add a Spring lifecycle timeout of 20 seconds.
• That does not mean every shutdown waits 20 seconds; it sets the maximum time allowed for a shutdown phase when work is still finishing.
• The important contrast is becoming clear: the CLI reports its final status directly, while the server lets the Spring lifecycle coordinate shutdown.

steps.title: Enable graceful server shutdown
steps.why:
• Now we tell the embedded web server to use graceful shutdown behavior.
• server.shutdown: graceful is a Spring Boot configuration setting, not a call to System.exit().
• When the application is stopped normally, Spring Boot and the embedded server coordinate the shutdown process.
• That gives active requests a chance to finish instead of a controller suddenly terminating the JVM for every user.
• So we now have two deliberate process policies in the same project.
• The standalone preflight CLI may return a non-zero process code at its outer boundary, while the long-running web service uses framework-managed graceful shutdown.

steps.title: Create empty DatasetPreflightValidatorTest.java
steps.why:
• Before we can type the real DatasetPreflightValidatorTest.java content, IntelliJ needs that file to exist in the GeoOps project.
• This step creates DatasetPreflightValidatorTest.java as an empty editor tab at src/test/java/com/atlasgrid/geoops/tools/preflight/DatasetPreflightValidatorTest.java.
• We deliberately leave DatasetPreflightValidatorTest.java blank here so the next lesson action can visibly type its source instead of making completed code appear all at once.
• When you move forward, watch DatasetPreflightValidatorTest.java fill in through IntelliJ's typeCode animation while the active code stays in view.

steps.title: Test exit-code decisions without killing the test JVM
steps.why:
• Before running the CLI itself, we test the validator as ordinary Java logic.
• This is exactly why we kept System.exit() out of DatasetPreflightValidator.
• If the validator called System.exit() internally, a unit test could terminate the entire Maven test process before JUnit finished running.
• @TempDir asks JUnit to create a temporary directory that the test can safely use for filesystem scenarios.
• The first test passes no dataset argument and checks for exit code 2.
• The second points to a file that does not exist and verifies exit code 3.
• The unsupported-type test creates survey.exe and checks that the validator returns code 5.
• The success test creates survey.geojson and verifies a valid result with exit code 0.
• None of these tests terminate the JVM because they are testing the decision data, not the CLI process boundary.
• That separation makes the code easier to test and gives future callers the freedom to handle validation failures differently.

steps.title: Run the preflight validator tests
steps.why:
• Now we run the four new validator tests through JUnit.
• A green result means each tested input produced the exit-code decision we expected.
• We are verifying codes 2, 3, 5, and 0 without ever calling System.exit() inside the test process.
• This gives us confidence in the reusable validation rules before we move to the real command-line boundary.

steps.title: Verify the complete GeoOps build after Set 2 changes
steps.why:
• The focused validator tests passed, but we also need to make sure Set 2 did not break the rest of GeoOps.
• Maven clean verify rebuilds the project from a clean target directory and runs the full test suite.
• At this point the suite contains the original Spring context test plus the four preflight validator tests.
• Seeing five tests pass and BUILD SUCCESS tells us the new CLI code and the existing web application can live in the same project without breaking each other.

steps.title: Start the long-running GeoOps web service again
steps.why:
• Before demonstrating the short-lived CLI, let's look again at the other kind of Java process in this project.
• GeoOpsApplication starts a Spring Boot web server that is expected to stay alive and keep serving HTTP requests.
• That is very different from the preflight tool, which performs one check and then ends.
• Starting the service here makes the process-boundary difference visible before we stop it gracefully.

data.console:

2026-09-29 INFO Tomcat started on port 8080 (http)

steps.title: Stop the web service through the Spring lifecycle
steps.why:
• Now we stop the server through its normal application lifecycle rather than calling System.exit() from business code.
• Because graceful shutdown is enabled, Spring Boot owns the shutdown sequence for this long-running service.
• The practical rule is simple: controllers and services should not decide to terminate the whole JVM just because one request or one business operation failed.
• Those layers should return errors or throw exceptions that the application can handle while the server continues serving other work.
• System.exit() stays reserved for a true process boundary such as our standalone preflight CLI.

steps.title: Open IntelliJ's integrated terminal
steps.why:
• Now we are switching from source code to the place where a command-line program is actually launched.
• The integrated terminal is a shell inside IntelliJ where we can type operating-system commands without leaving the IDE.
• The master simulator keeps command typing visible here and uses a yellow boundary around the current command.
• That matters for this lesson because we want to see both the command being executed and the exit code returned by the process.

steps.title: Run the CLI with no dataset argument
steps.why:
• First we intentionally run the preflight CLI incorrectly by providing no dataset path.
• The Java command launches GeoOpsPreflightCli from the compiled target/classes directory.
• Because main() receives an empty args array, DatasetPreflightValidator returns the usage failure with exit code 2.
• The CLI prints the usage message and then System.exit(2) ends this short-lived Java process.
• The terminal remains open because IntelliJ itself is not being terminated; only the Java process that ran the CLI has ended.
• That distinction is one of the most important things to understand about System.exit().

steps.title: Run the CLI with a missing GIS file
steps.why:
• This time we provide a dataset path, but the file does not exist.
• The argument reaches Path.of(), and Files.exists() returns false.
• The validator chooses exit code 3 and returns that decision as a PreflightResult.
• Only after the result reaches GeoOpsPreflightCli does System.exit(3) terminate the CLI process.
• The yellow command boundary keeps the exact command visible while the terminal also shows the non-zero exit status.

steps.title: See an unsupported dataset return exit code 5
steps.why:
• Now we simulate a file that exists but has a type our preflight tool does not support.
• The command creates survey.exe and immediately passes that path into the CLI.
• Because .exe is not in the supported extension set, validation returns exit code 5.
• This shows why different non-zero codes can be useful: an automation script can distinguish incorrect usage, missing files, and unsupported formats instead of receiving one vague failure value.

steps.title: See a valid GeoJSON preflight finish with exit code 0
steps.why:
• Finally we create a GeoJSON file and pass it to the same CLI.
• The file exists, it is a regular file, and its .geojson extension is supported.
• The validator therefore returns PreflightResult.success() with exit code 0.
• GeoOpsPreflightCli prints the success message and returns naturally from main() instead of calling System.exit(0).
• The operating system still sees a successful exit code because normal completion of main() ends the Java process successfully.
• We have now demonstrated the full process policy in a real terminal flow: successful work ends normally, while known failures use explicit non-zero exit codes at the outer CLI boundary.

• The behavior is working, so now we review exactly what Set 2 changed before recording it in history.

• Keeping this as a separate Set 2 commit makes the project evolution easy to inspect later.
• We can clearly see which files introduced process-exit behavior instead of mixing them invisibly into the original bootstrap commit.

steps.title: Stage the Set 2 process-boundary changes
steps.why:
• We stage the Set 2 files after reviewing them.
• The staging area now represents one coherent change: add a testable GIS preflight CLI, keep System.exit() at the outer process boundary, and configure the web service for graceful shutdown.
• That is the exact change we want the next commit to describe.

steps.title: Commit the controlled System.exit() design
steps.why:
• Now we record Set 2 as its own Git milestone.
• The commit message describes the design rather than merely listing filenames.
• This gives later sets a clean point in history where GeoOps gained a second process type: the long-running web service plus a short-lived operational CLI.

• That final automation check is important because the preflight tests and the original Spring Boot test must all pass together on a clean runner.
